title: Intraosseous access in neonates
subject: paediatrics
setting: Delivery room, emergency department, SNCU, NICU, transport
summary: Emergency route for drugs and fluids when umbilical venous or peripheral access fails. Use the flat anteromedial proximal tibia 1 to 2 cm below and 1 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity, stop at the loss of resistance, watch the limb for extravasation and remove the needle as soon as other access is secured.

sections.title: When to use IO
items: At birth the umbilical vein is the primary emergency access; if umbilical venous access is not feasible, or the baby is outside the delivery room, IO is a reasonable alternative (ERC, weak recommendation, very low certainty evidence).
Place an IO if venous access cannot be secured within three attempts and within 90 seconds.
IO can be used in preterm and term neonates, and all intravenous medications can be given by this route.
After resuscitation, IO access may be sufficient in the short term if no other site is available.

sections.title: Site and insertion
items: Preferred site: proximal tibia, flat anteromedial surface 1 to 2 cm below and 1 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity. NRP 8th edition describes about 2 cm distal and 1 to 2 cm medial.
If the tuberosity cannot be felt, use the flat medial tibia 1.5 to 2 cm distal to the patella.
Second site: distal femur, anterior midline, 1 to 3 cm above the external condyles.

Keep clear of the growth plate: an ultrasound study aimed for at least 10 mm from it, and a puncture 10 mm below the tuberosity breached that margin in 53% of proximal sites. At 3000 to 4000 g the most suitable site was a median 13.0 mm below the tuberosity.
Insert the needle perpendicular to the skin through periosteum and cortex, and stop at the loss of resistance that marks entry into the marrow cavity.
In neonatal cadavers, manually inserted needles leaked less than drill-assisted ones and depth needed adjusting for birth weight; contrast leaked in 15.8% overall and 41.7% of VLBW infants.

sections.title: After insertion
items: Watch the limb for swelling, extravasation and poor perfusion throughout every infusion.
Remove the IO line once alternative venous access is secured.

sections.title: Complications and pitfalls
items: German surveillance of 161 neonates: IO access succeeded in 91%, at the first attempt in 75%; severe complications occurred in 6%.

Severe complications (about 6%): necrosis, fracture, broken needle, osteomyelitis, soft tissue infection and perfusion problems. Minor (about 30%): soft tissue misplacement, mild paravasation, poor healing and local swelling.
Reported serious events include tibial fracture, osteomyelitis, and extravasation causing compartment syndrome and amputation.
Neonatal staff rarely train on IO devices; regular role-appropriate training is needed.
